family: Your own car's factory unit — the sleeper build
examples: The head unit currently in your dashboard
A second-hand one for your exact model, so you keep the original
one_liner: The only route to a deck that looks like it left the factory.

price.v: £15–60 for a used unit for your model
price.why: ⚠️ Buy a SECOND one rather than gutting the one in your car. If the build stalls you still have a working radio, and if you sell the car you can put it back.

window_w_mm.why: OEM windows are usually SMALL — a segment display for frequency and track number. Measure before committing to this route.

chassis.why: Some are a standard 1-DIN box in a car-specific surround; some are car-specific throughout. Yours decides how much of this project applies.

cage_included.v: usually not — OEM units bolt to car-specific brackets
cage_included.why: This is the big structural difference from an aftermarket donor and it is easy to overlook.

buttons.v: varies; often fewer than an aftermarket unit
buttons.why: Count them before choosing this route — you want six.

knob.why: The reason to do this at all: it matches the rest of the interior.

display_tech.why: ⚠️ Many OEM units of the right era use a VFD. Treat the power board as live.

why: The fascia already fits your dashboard exactly, because it was made for it. No adapter, no gap, no aftermarket look.
The knobs, the button shapes and the texture match the rest of the interior, which nothing bought will.
It is the only route where somebody looking at the dash does not immediately see that something has been changed.
watch_out: ⚠️ The window is usually far too small, and enlarging an OEM fascia destroys the exact thing you chose it for. Measure FIRST — this route is only worth it if the window is usable or the fascia can take a clean new aperture.
OEM units often have no cage, bolting to car-specific brackets instead. You may keep the brackets and lose the cage.
Car-specific means single-source: if you break the fascia, there is no generic replacement.
⚠️ Do not gut the unit currently in your car. Buy a second.
steps: Check your car's entry in docs/VEHICLES.md first — it tells you what the aperture and harness are before you buy anything.
Buy a second-hand unit for your exact model rather than removing yours.
Measure the window before any disassembly. If it will not take 76 × 19 mm, decide now whether you are cutting it or choosing a different route.
Note how it mounts — brackets or cage — because that decides the chassis you build.
Then the standard teardown: fascia first, keep every screw.

teardown.note: The reason you chose this route. Car-specific and single-source — break it and there is no generic replacement.
Often fewer than an aftermarket unit. Count before committing.
⚠️ OEM units usually bolt to these rather than sliding into a cage. They ARE your mounting.
⚠️ Many OEM units of the right era use a VFD. Treat the power board as live.
Discharge. OEM amps are often integrated into the main board — cut carefully.
⚠️ On some cars this also handles chimes or the clock. Losing it may be more than losing a radio.
Varies entirely by manufacturer — some are a standard box in a car-specific surround, some are not.

reuse.value: £12–20 and a part you would otherwise buy
reuse.note: ⚠️ THE BIG ONE. Every CD-era head unit contains a 4-channel amplifier — usually a TDA7388, TDA7850 or similar — already bolted to the chassis as its heatsink and already wired to the ISO speaker connector. That is exactly the part BUILD.md tells you to go and buy. Cut the amp IC's four inputs free of the dead preamp and inject the deck's line out there instead. The IC datasheet gives the pinout; the mute/standby pin usually needs tying to its enable level, and that is the step people miss.

reuse.value: hard to buy in the right shape
reuse.note: On most units the amplifier's heatsink IS part of the chassis casting. If you reuse the amp you get it for nothing; if you fit your own amp board, bolting it to the same casting is free cooling.

reuse.value: a pound, and some peace of mind
reuse.note: The reverse-polarity diode, the input fuse holder and the filter capacitors on the donor's power input are already rated for a car's supply. Cheap to buy, but they are already there and already fused.

reuse.value: an adapter you would otherwise buy
reuse.note: ✅ Better than an ISO block: the donor already has YOUR car's exact connector on it, so keeping the back panel means no harness adapter at all. This is a real advantage of the OEM route that the fascia usually gets all the credit for.
⚠️ Same problem as any donor and usually worse — OEM displays are small, segment-based and custom. Measure and identify before hoping.
